title: Practical & Algorithmic Coding
description: Realistic coding interview prompts (full-stack, concurrency, data structures, parsers) with starter code and runnable test suites.

questions.title: LRU Cache with Per-Key TTL
questions.prompt: Implement an in-memory cache `TTLLRUCache(capacity)` supporting `get(key, now_ms)` and `put(key, value, ttl_ms, now_ms)` in O(1) average time. Expired entries must not be returned by `get` and should be evicted before live entries when at capacity.

tests.python:
c = TTLLRUCache(2)
c.put('a', 1, 100, 0)
c.put('b', 2, 500, 10)
assert c.get('a', 50) == 1
assert c.get('a', 100) is None  # expired at 100
c.put('c', 3, 500, 120)         # 'a' is expired, 'b' must stay
assert c.get('b', 130) == 2
assert c.get('c', 130) == 3
c.put('d', 4, 500, 140)         # full with two live entries: 'b' is least recently used
assert c.get('d', 150) == 4
assert c.get('b', 150) is None
assert c.get('c', 150) == 3
print('ALL TESTS PASSED')

hints: Think about separating recency tracking (OrderedDict / Map) from lazy vs. proactive expiration.
Edge cases: capacity=0, updating an existing key with a new TTL, ttl_ms <= 0.

questions.title: Sliding-Window Rate Limiter
questions.prompt: Implement `RateLimiter(limit, window_ms)` with `allow(user_id, now_ms) -> bool` that permits at most `limit` requests per user in any rolling `window_ms` interval `(now_ms - window_ms, now_ms]`. Follow-up: how would you bound memory across millions of idle users?

tests.python:
rl = RateLimiter(2, 1000)
assert rl.allow('u1', 100) is True
assert rl.allow('u1', 500) is True
assert rl.allow('u1', 900) is False
assert rl.allow('u2', 900) is True
assert rl.allow('u1', 1100) is True   # 100 fell out of (100, 1100]
assert rl.allow('u1', 1200) is False
print('ALL TESTS PASSED')

hints: Use a per-user deque and evict timestamps <= now_ms - window_ms.
Only append a timestamp when the request is allowed — rejected requests shouldn't consume quota!

questions.title: Incremental SSE Stream Parser
questions.prompt: Write an incremental Server-Sent Events parser `SSEParser` with `feed(chunk: str) -> list[dict]` that handles arbitrary chunk boundaries (including splits mid-line or mid-CRLF), `event:` and multi-line `data:` fields, comments starting with `:`, and blank-line event dispatch.

tests.python:
p = SSEParser()
assert p.feed('event: delta
da') == []
assert p.feed('ta: hello
data: world

') == [{'event': 'delta', 'data': 'hello
world'}]
assert p.feed(': keepalive
data: solo

') == [{'event': 'message', 'data': 'solo'}]
print('ALL TESTS PASSED')

hints: Keep a trailing line buffer for incomplete lines without a newline.
Watch out for CRLF split across two chunks ('\r' at end of chunk 1, '\n' at start of chunk 2) and optional single leading space after ':'.

questions.title: Transactional Text Buffer with Undo / Redo
questions.prompt: Implement `TextEditor` supporting `insert(pos, text)`, `delete(pos, length)`, `undo()`, `redo()`, and `get_text() -> str`. Calling `insert` or `delete` after an `undo()` must clear the redo stack. Out-of-bounds positions should be clamped safely.

tests.python:
ed = TextEditor()
ed.insert(0, 'hello world')
assert ed.delete(5, 6) == ' world'
assert ed.get_text() == 'hello'
assert ed.undo() is True
assert ed.get_text() == 'hello world'
assert ed.redo() is True
assert ed.get_text() == 'hello'
ed.undo()
ed.insert(5, '!')
assert ed.get_text() == 'hello! world'
assert ed.redo() is False
print('ALL TESTS PASSED')

hints: Store minimal inverse command records rather than full document snapshots so memory scales with edit size.
Follow-up discussion: how would you coalesce rapid keystrokes or support collaborative undo?

questions.title: Bounded-Concurrency Async Batch Runner
questions.prompt: Implement `run_with_limit(items, worker, limit)` (or `runWithLimit` in JS) that runs an async `worker(item)` over `items` with at most `limit` concurrent executions, preserves input order in the returned results list, and fails fast if any worker throws.

starter_code.python:
import asyncio

async def run_with_limit(items, worker, limit: int):
    pass

tests.python:
import asyncio
active = 0
peak = 0
async def w(x):
    global active, peak
    active += 1
    peak = max(peak, active)
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    active -= 1
    return x * 10
res = await run_with_limit([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], w, 2)
assert res == [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], f'got {res}'
assert peak <= 2, f'peak concurrency {peak} > 2'
async def failing_worker(x):
    if x == 2:
        raise RuntimeError('boom')
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return x
failed = False
try:
    await run_with_limit([1, 2, 3], failing_worker, 2)
except RuntimeError:
    failed = True
assert failed, 'expected fail-fast exception propagation'
print('ALL TESTS PASSED')

hints: A semaphore or fixed pool of `min(limit, len(items))` worker coroutines pulling from a shared index works cleanly.
Discuss cancellation semantics on failure and backpressure when `items` is an iterator of 1M elements.

questions.title: Transactional Key-Value Store with Nested Transactions
questions.prompt: Implement `TransactionalKV` supporting `set(k, v)`, `get(k)`, `delete(k)`, `begin()`, `commit()`, and `rollback()`. Transactions can be nested arbitrarily deep; `commit()` applies only the innermost transaction to its parent (or base store), while `rollback()` discards only the innermost transaction.

tests.python:
kv = TransactionalKV()
kv.set('a', 1)
kv.begin()
kv.set('a', 2)
kv.begin()
kv.delete('a')
assert kv.get('a') is None
assert kv.rollback() is True
assert kv.get('a') == 2
assert kv.commit() is True
assert kv.get('a') == 2
assert kv.rollback() is False
print('ALL TESTS PASSED')

hints: Use a stack of delta frames with a distinct TOMBSTONE sentinel for deletions inside a transaction.
Make sure deleting a key inside an inner transaction masks the outer value instead of falling through!
